title: Decidability of branching-VASS reachability
formal: Is there an algorithm deciding reachability in branching vector addition systems with states when the dimension is part of the input? Given a finite system \(B\) as defined below and a target configuration \(q(x)\), decide whether \(q(x)\) is the root of a finite valid derivation tree of \(B\).
why: Branching VASS extend the Petri-net style of counter computation to recursive combinations of resources. Settling exact reachability in arbitrary dimension would identify a central decidability boundary between path computations and branching derivations in infinite-state verification.
status_note: Rechecked on 16 September 2026 against Bizière–Leroux–Sutre arXiv:2609.15869v1, the extended FOSSACS 2026 paper posted 14 September. Its introduction and conclusion explicitly retain arbitrary-dimensional BVASS reachability as open. Theorem 5.2 represents reachability sets as VASS sections without a general effective construction; Remark 5.4 and §6 distinguish existence of a structural bound from a computable bound. Theorem 7.3 handles two-dimensional BVASS and five-dimensional single-state BVAS, not five-dimensional arbitrary-state BVASS. No matching resolution is claimed by this new source. The formal target and the 2025 source conventions are retained; source theorem scopes were checked, not every proof independently certified.

importance.reason: A core decidability question for a major extension of vector addition systems, left open beyond recent low-dimensional progress and closely connected to resource-sensitive computation.

sentences: A branching vector addition system combines finite control with nonnegative integer resources.
Rules can combine several already derived configurations by adding their resource vectors and a fixed displacement.
Reachability asks whether a finite valid derivation tree produces exactly a supplied target.
The dimension is part of the input, and every branch must be fully justified.
The September 2026 structural and low-dimensional results explicitly leave arbitrary-dimensional reachability open.

definitions: The input dimension is an integer \(d\geq1\). A \(d\)-dimensional branching vector addition system with states (\(d\)-BVASS) has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\) and finite rules \((S,a,q)\), where \(S\subseteq Q\), \(a\in\mathbb Z^d\) and \(q\in Q\). A configuration \(q(x)\) consists of a state \(q\) and vector \(x\in\mathbb N^d\). A rule with \(S=\{q_1,\ldots,q_k\}\) combines one configuration \(q_i(x_i)\) for each input state into \(q(a+x_1+\cdots+x_k)\), provided all coordinates of this output are nonnegative. All child configurations must themselves have nonnegative coordinates. Input states in one rule are distinct, following the source’s set convention. When \(S\) is empty, the rule supplies the initial configuration \(q(a)\) if \(a\geq0\) coordinatewise. A derivation is a finite rooted tree: each node uses one rule, has exactly its rule’s specified children, and its label is obtained by the preceding sum. Leaves therefore use empty-input rules. A target is reachable if some such tree has that target as root. Derivations may use the same rule any finite number of times; there is no global stock of initial tokens shared between different branches. The number of children and the dimension are unbounded input parameters. States, rules, child-state sets and target are listed explicitly, with signed binary integers for displacement coordinates and binary nonnegative target coordinates. There are no equality or zero tests, resets, counter multiplication, probability or additional acceptance conditions. Decidability means one deterministic Turing machine that halts and answers correctly on every valid finite encoding, with no running-time bound requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating algorithm for the stated arbitrary-dimensional finite-tree reachability problem, or prove in Lean that it is undecidable. A dimension-dependent result covering only some fixed dimensions, a coverability algorithm, or a procedure that terminates only on reachable targets does not decide this problem. Finite derivation trees must satisfy every branch and every exact target coordinate.

context_blocks.text: A unary rule follows one computation, while a branching rule combines completed subcomputations by adding their counter vectors. For example, in one dimension, initial rules yielding \(p(2)\) and \(q(3)\) together with a zero-displacement rule from \(\{p,q\}\) to \(r\) derive \(r(5)\). Both child computations are required.

Ordinary VASS are the fragment using only initial and unary rules. Their reachability is decidable. Branching changes paths into finite derivation trees, so ordinary reachability decidability does not automatically extend to the system in this card.

Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove decidability in dimension two in 2025. They obtain an effectively computable semilinear description of the reachable set: a finite union, for each state, of sets consisting of a base vector plus arbitrary nonnegative integer combinations of finitely many period vectors.

The paper explicitly leaves reachability open in arbitrary dimension. It also cautions that its two-dimensional procedure does not provide a complexity upper bound. Decidability in every input dimension is therefore the main target here, rather than an optimization of the two-dimensional running time.

Reachability requires exactly the requested counter vector. Coverability would allow a vector above it coordinatewise and can discard information crucial to exact reachability. Similarly, a derivation that leaves a branch unresolved is not a valid witness.

Since every finite proposed tree can be checked, positive instances have finite verifiable witnesses. This alone gives no way to halt on every negative instance. The question is precisely whether an always-terminating decision procedure exists.

The extended FOSSACS 2026 paper proves that every BVASS reachability set is a section of a VASS reachability set: one intersects with specified semilinear constraints and projects selected counters. The theorem is a structural existence statement. The paper does not obtain a general effective construction that would turn it into a reachability decider, and Remark 5.4 explicitly explains this distinction.

Its low-dimensional result gives effectively semilinear reachability sets for two-dimensional BVASS and five-dimensional BVAS. A BVAS here is the single-control-state version, so the five-dimensional theorem must not be attributed to arbitrary-state BVASS. The conclusion again identifies arbitrary-dimensional exact reachability as open. The retained 2025 rule conventions and decision target are unchanged.
